hints: Focus on where a competitive inhibitor binds on this enzyme, and what it is competing with for that spot.
Remember that $K_m$ is the substrate concentration needed to reach half of $V_{max}$, so ask yourself what happens to both values when extra substrate can outcompete the inhibitor.
walkthrough:
**Remind yourself what $K_m$ and $V_{max}$ mean**

Think of $V_{max}$ as the flat top of your curve, the fastest rate when every active site is full.
Think of $K_m$ as the substrate concentration that gives half of $V_{max}$. A low $K_m$ means high affinity, because you need only a little substrate to work well.

**Picture how a competitive inhibitor works**

A competitive inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate, so it fits reversibly into the active site and blocks it.
It does not change the enzyme permanently, it just gets in the way. If you add lots more substrate, the substrate wins the competition.

**Predict the new curve**

At low substrate, rate is lower because many active sites are blocked, so you need more substrate to reach half $V_{max}$. That means $K_m$ increases.
At very high substrate concentration, the inhibitor is outcompeted and all sites can still be filled, so the same flat top is reached:
$$V_{max} \text{ with inhibitor} = V_{max} \text{ without inhibitor}$$

options.A: Km does increase, but Vmax does not decrease. A lower Vmax that cannot be overcome is the sign of non-competitive inhibition, not competitive.
options.B: Correct. More substrate is needed for half Vmax so Km increases, but high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor so the same Vmax is still reached.
options.C: This is backwards. Unchanged Km with decreased Vmax describes non-competitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds elsewhere and cannot be outcompeted.
options.D: The inhibitor must have some effect. Competitive inhibition lowers apparent affinity, so Km cannot stay the same even though Vmax does.
